title: T/F/NI + Vocabulary: Drilling for Memory (poziom wojewodzki)

tasks.instruction: Przeczytaj ponizszy tekst. Zdecyduj, ktore zdania (1.1.–1.5.) sa zgodne z trescia tekstu (T – True), ktore sa niezgodne (F – False), a ktore zawieraja informacje niepodane w tekscie (NI – No Information). Nastepnie znajdz w tekscie wyrazy lub wyrazenia, ktore odpowiadaja definicjom podanym w punktach 1.6.–1.10. Wymagana jest calkowita poprawnosc ortograficzna odpowiedzi.
tasks.text:
DRILLING FOR MEMORY

At four and a half thousand metres on Mont Blanc, in a season that allows perhaps three weeks of work, a small team spends its days pulling cylinders of ice out of a glacier and packing them into insulated boxes. The ice is not going to a laboratory. Most of it is going into a cave dug beneath the snow in Antarctica, where it will sit at minus fifty degrees, unopened, waiting for scientists who have not yet been born.

The drilling itself is unglamorous. A hollow bit turns slowly down into the ice and brings up a cylinder about ten centimetres across and a metre long; each one is measured, labelled, wrapped and stacked, and the hole goes deeper. At that altitude, in a tent, with a generator that objects to the cold, a good day produces perhaps twenty metres. The team works in short shifts, because nobody thinks clearly for long that high up, and the whole operation has to be lifted off the mountain by helicopter before the weather closes in. Getting the cores down without letting them warm is more difficult than getting them out in the first place: a core that thaws even briefly on the journey is no longer evidence of anything.

The logic is straightforward and slightly bleak. A glacier is an archive. Snow that fell two centuries ago is now compressed ice a hundred metres down, and trapped inside it are bubbles of the air of that year, together with dust, pollen, ash from distant volcanoes and the chemical traces of whatever human beings happened to be burning at the time. Read carefully, a core drilled from the right glacier gives a year-by-year account of the atmosphere going back, in the deepest Antarctic samples, several hundred thousand years.

Mountain glaciers hold a different and in some ways more useful record: local, detailed, and closely connected to the places where people actually live. They are also melting. Once meltwater begins to percolate down through the ice it redistributes the chemistry, and the archive is not so much destroyed as scrambled - which is worse, because a scrambled record can still be measured, and can therefore be misread. Several of the glaciers on the project's original list have already been judged beyond use.

Hence the cave. The founders argued that the sensible response to an archive burning down is to carry out what you can before the fire reaches it, even if you have no immediate use for the documents. Analytical techniques improve constantly, and the instruments of the 2070s will be able to ask questions of a core drilled today that nobody can currently formulate. Storing the ice in Antarctica rather than in a freezer at a university has an obvious appeal: no power supply is required, and no funding decision taken in a difficult budget year can accidentally switch it off.

What records of this kind have already produced is not in dispute. Ice from the Alps carries the lead released by Roman smelting, a sharp rise from the leaded petrol of the twentieth century and its retreat after the bans that followed; cores from the Andes hold the ash of eruptions that appear in no written source; the long Antarctic samples established the relationship between carbon dioxide and temperature across eight ice ages, which is the backbone of a great deal that has been argued since. Every one of those findings was made with instruments that did not exist on the day the ice came out of the ground.

The undertaking is not without its critics. Drilling and shipping ice from remote mountains is expensive and, awkwardly for a climate project, not free of carbon. Some glaciologists argue that the same money would deliver more if it were spent analysing cores now, with the instruments that exist, rather than betting on future ones. The founders' answer is that the two are not really alternatives, and that the deadline is not negotiable. A grant application can be submitted again next year. A glacier that has melted cannot.

items.statement: Most of the ice removed on Mont Blanc is analysed as soon as it reaches a laboratory.
items.explanation: FALSE - 'The ice is not going to a laboratory'; most of it goes unopened into a cave in Antarctica.

items.statement: Meltwater passing through a glacier makes its record misleading rather than simply removing it.
items.explanation: TRUE - The archive 'is not so much destroyed as scrambled - which is worse, because a scrambled record can still be measured, and can therefore be misread'.

items.statement: The Antarctic store was chosen partly because it needs no electricity.
items.explanation: TRUE - 'No power supply is required, and no funding decision taken in a difficult budget year can accidentally switch it off'.

items.statement: All the glaciers the project originally selected have now been drilled.
items.explanation: FALSE - 'Several of the glaciers on the project's original list have already been judged beyond use'.

items.statement: The project is paid for mainly by private donations.
items.explanation: NO INFORMATION - Grant applications and budget years are mentioned, but the text never says where the money comes from.
